summary: W3C Geolocation is a browser scripting interface that gives a web page the geographic position of the device it runs on, once the user has granted permission. It reports latitude, longitude, altitude, speed and heading, with accuracy figures and a time stamp, in the World Geodetic System 1984 frame, either once or as repeated updates when the position changes significantly. It leaves scenes, avatars, networking, identity and the anchoring of content to a place to other standards, and it defines no markup language and no new address scheme for places. A standards audience should know that the heading is the direction of travel and not the way the device faces, that the specification gives no guarantee the position is the device's actual location, and that the interface is available only in secure contexts.

sources.title: Geolocation, 9.3 heading attribute
sources.quote: The heading attribute denotes the direction of travel of the hosting device and is specified in degrees, where 0° ≤ heading < 360°, counting clockwise relative to the true north.

sources.title: Geolocation, 9.2 altitude and altitudeAccuracy attributes
sources.quote: The altitude attribute denotes the height of the position, specified in meters above the [ WGS84 ] ellipsoid.

coverage.note: The specification fixes one frame for every position it reports, the World Geodetic System 1984 coordinate system, with altitude measured above its ellipsoid; it offers no way to declare a different frame.

sources.title: Geolocation, 9.1 latitude, longitude, and accuracy attributes

coverage.note: Position is released to a page only after the user grants permission, in secure contexts, and under a permissions policy whose default allows only the same origin; recipients are advised to use the data only for its task. Missing: spatial coarsening and machine-readable use or retention declarations; the recipient guidance is non-normative.

sources.title: Geolocation, 3.1 User consent
sources.quote: Geolocation is a powerful feature that requires express permission from an end-user before any location data is shared with a web application.

sources.title: Geolocation, 3.2 Privacy considerations for recipients of location information
sources.quote: Recipients ought to only request position information when necessary, and only use the location information for the task for which it was provided to them.

sources.title: Geolocation, D. Change log
sources.quote: The API is now only exposed in Secure Contexts (i.e., only available in HTTPS).
